subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH PROPOSED AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the ordinary
course of events I would readily concur in the suggestion, but we were assured that all the legislation that we would have to consider was before us. Amendments to the elections act should not be suddenly hurried through in the closing days of this session. I know that there is one reason put forward why it should be considered, but when it was indicated to me that this course might be followed I stated the objection I would have. It was indicated that it was hoped to hold a municipal election in the Northwest Territories. However, that would only call for a single amendment to the elections act as it stands. I would readily concur in the introduction of that amendment so that the election in question could, be proceeded with without delay, but I want to make it clear that consideration of amendments to an act as important as this should not be rushed.
It is true that amendments to the act have been considered by a committee, but there are a number of provisions in the act, relating not only to content but also to the form and wording of the sections, which might easily involve considerable discussion. For that reason, while I am most anxious to facilitate the business of the house, I do not propose to let the desire to complete that business interfere with adequate discussion of legislation coming before us.
I will agree to the introduction of notice of an amendment simply to provide for the municipal election which is under discussion, but I regret I cannot agree to any motion which would seek to bring before us at this time the whole elections act unless it is understood that we shall continue to sit for some considerable time to deal with it.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 403, to establish national standards for dairy products and to regulate interprovincial and international trade in dairy products.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
Before the clause carries I should like to say a few words with regard to this matter. I am disappointed that the bill is brought forward at this late stage in the session. The bill should have gone before the standing committee on agriculture, and producer representatives should have been called to discuss the measure. It seems to me it is a mistake to bring in the bill at this late date, because it is an important measure so far as the dairy industry of Canada is concerned. It sets out the regulations under which we are going to be able to trade inter-provincially in dairy products. It sets out the standards that are to be required for dairy products in Canada, and it seems to me that the producers of those dairy products should have been called before a committee of the house to consider the matter.
So far as the producers are concerned, I have heard quite a few complaints from them in eastern Canada with respect to the undergrading of dairy products, especially cream. Individual producers are not able to get separate returns showing what their particular grades are. The product goes from the producer to the dairy and is graded there. Government graders check the grades, but
Canada Dairy Products Act the individual producer is not able to get a return with respect to his product, except the one that comes from the company purchasing his product. He is not able to get a return of the grade made by the government inspector. I know that the dairy producers of eastern Canada have been making inquiries about this matter, and that they want some changes made in the act to allow the individual producer, or the producers' representative, to obtain a return showing the grade of their particular product. They also want some method by which they can ascertain whether the grades set by the government inspectors are carried through to the ultimate consumers, and also information as to the amount of the product manufactured when they ship cream to the dairies.
A farmer gets back a test saying the butter-fat content of his cream was 30 per cent or 40 per cent or whatever it may be, but there is nothing from the manufacturer showing that the percentage indicated represents the amount of butterfat for which he has paid the producers. I know it is not the same as with grain in western Canada, where you can follow it right through. These products are being manufactured, but under the act today there is no check on the amount of butter-fat finally produced and disposed of in the form of the manufactured product. It seems to me there should be some provision in the act compelling the manufacturer to produce returns to show he was not selling a greater amount of butterfat than he was buying from the producers. It should also be possible to see that when the producer is paid on first grade cream, that grade is carried through to the consumer.
I do not think any hon. member has been able to give this bill the consideration it should have. It was on our desks when we came down this morning; we have had about two minutes to look at it, and now we are supposed to deal intelligently with it. I believe that is a mistake. This bill should should have been sent, or should be sent even now, to the agriculture committee, where it could be given proper consideration.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
On the first question as to consultation, the reason the bill has not been brought in until late in the session is that all parties have been consulted continuously. As will be recalled, this matter was up at the dominion-provincial agricultural meeting last December, and on that occasion we were asked to submit it to the provinces and the dairy organizations right across Canada. That has been done, and the consent of those organizations has been given to this type of legislation.

Canada Dairy Products Act

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Was there unanimous agreement among the producers?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
So far as I know, there have been no objections to the legislation. It is the only kind of legislation we can have under the circumstances. The legislation we had previously was entirely satisfactory to everyone in the dairy industry and to the various departments of agriculture across the country, but the court decision rendered that type of legislation of no effect. It is most important that there should be legislation on the statute book which is not ultra vires, and this legislation is considered to be intra vires. Of course there is nothing to prevent its being amended in succeeding sessions if any difficulty is found with it, but it does not cover the points just raised by the hon. member for Melfort. All those points are dealt with in provincial legislation; they are not covered by this legislation at all.
When a farmer in Ontario takes his cream to a creamery in this province, all matters relating to it, including grades and everything else, are dealt with in the provincial legislation. All the provincial and dominion legislation provides that we appoint the provincial inspectors as our inspectors under this act; the provinces in turn appoint our inspectors as their inspectors under their acts, and they work in co-operation. The provincial inspectors deal with intraprovincial matters such as the grading of the cream or butter or milk for use within the province, and we touch it only when it becomes interprovincial or international trade. This legislation makes that possible.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: But this legislation sets the standards that must be maintained by any product when it goes into interprovincial or export trade.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Only if it goes into interprovincial or export trade. As long as the trade is within the province this does not affect it.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: But quantities of these products are exported between the provinces; therefore the standards across the dominion must be the same, which in effect means that the regulations made under this act establish the grades for the dominion.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
There is nothing that says
they must be the same across the dominion. The provincial acts set out the grades for each province. By agreement we have tried to make them the same, and to all intents and purposes they are the same.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
I had intended to speak at some length in support of the arguments presented by the hon. member for Melfort, but in view


of the explanations given by the minister and his suggestion that if the act is not satisfactory it can be amended later, I will not take the time of the committee to do so.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On section 6-Export or import of substitutes.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Will the minister explain the meaning of this section? It would appear to prohibit the movement of a manufactured substitute such as margarine from one province to another, if the minister chose to do so.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
That provision is now in
the law, that we can prohibit the importation of substitutes for butter or the movement of substitutes from one province to another. That is necessary because of the fact that at the moment Quebec and Prince Edward Island prohibit the manufacture and sale of substitutes. This gives us authority to enforce the wishes of the various provinces in that regard.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
I am very sorry this
bill has been brought in. Representing an important rural dairy riding I came to the chamber in such a hurry that I forgot my glasses and have had to send for them. I presume a draft of this bill has been sent to the ministers of agriculture of the various provinces. Perhaps I should be abrupt and come right to the point. Is this going to facilitate in any shape or form the increased production of an imitation of a natural dairy product, such as margarine? In particular, will it in any way facilitate the importation of this product or any of its ingredients from other countries?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
The bill does not change
the position in any way in relation to the importation of substitutes. Margarine has never been mentioned as a product either in this bill or in the act. The term used is "substitutes for butter", and substitutes are in exactly the same position as before, in that they could not be imported into Canada. There is other legislation dealing with imports which makes more specific provision, but so far as this act is concerned there is no change in that regard. This act has to do with the decision made first by the Supreme Court of Canada and then by the privy council to the effect that this parliament has no authority to prohibit the manufacture and sale within the provinces of substitutes for butter. That is an authority which rests with the provinces. All we have done is to take out those parts on which we had no

authority in the first place; and if the provinces desire to pass them, they may do so. The province of Quebec has already done so, and so has Prince Edward Island. The other provinces can do the same thing if they so desire.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
I am glad to see that
others are coming to the defence of the dairy industry. Will this give the provinces the right, if they so desire or decide, to take the action the province of Quebec has already taken?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
The supreme court and the
privy council have decided they have that right. This measure does not say anything about it; but they have the right under the constitution.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
Exactly what is this
measure for, if it is not going to protect the dairymen?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: It does protect the dairymen to the extent that it makes it possible to exclude the importation of these products.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
I am sorry to carry the
discussion further, but from what the minister has said, my understanding is that it does permit the exclusion of the importation of these so-called substitutes for natural butter; is that correct?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Yes, the bill as it is drafted does that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: You say it does that?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: Would the minister explain the constitutional aspect of trading between the provinces? If shipments of margarine can be prevented from, let us say, Ontario to British Columbia, there must be some trade barrier which can be created by regulation.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: I am not a constitutional lawyer, but it is my understanding that that question was settled some years ago in connection with shipments of liquor from one province to another, and that there are certain set conditions under which it can or cannot be done. The same principle applies in this instance.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
May I suggest that the same principle would not be effective? Shipments of liquor from one province to another is prohibited by provincial law. In this instance we are endeavouring to state in a federal law what a province can do. While I am not prepared to say that I am a great constitutional lawyer, it does strike me that in this measure we are putting up barriers between provinces, and possibly doing so without proper jurisdiction.
Canada Dairy Products Act

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: It would only be where a province has taken action that we would take action under this legislation.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: I understand that the proper law officers have approved this bill. However, for forty years the dairymen of Canada were protected, as I understood it, by legislation similar to this. Then, out of the blue, the privy council said that the dairymen should not be further protected. Has this legislation been referred to the supreme court for its decision?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: This legislation has been before the law officers, and has been drafted in the light of the decision made by the privy council. As I understand it, all the privy council said in connection with this matter was that we had no right to say that a substitute for butter could not be manufactured in a province and sold in a province. They have said we had no right to say it-and for exactly the same reasons as I gave a moment ago, that we have no right to interfere with the grading of butter in a creamery in Ontario. That is a matter for Ontario. It is only when there is shipment of a product from one province to another or from this country to another country that we have anything to do with it. That latter power is all left with us; this bill still provides for our doing what we did under that power before.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: One more question; quite frankly I am very careful about any bill affecting the dairymen, after the deal they got in the last two or three years through a decision of some people over in England who knew nothing at all about farming in Canada. If any provincial department of agriculture tests this bill, will it be referred to the supreme court for decision?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext: My understanding is that if any provincial government desires to prevent the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine within its own province, it has the right to do so, in accordance with the decision of the privy council and also the decision of our own supreme court before the case was taken to the privy council. Any province that desires to stop it can stop it. As I said a moment ago, Quebec and Prince Edward Island have already done so. The other provinces may do so if they so desire.

I know this bill must have been designed to protect the dairymen, but I must say I am sceptical, because the dairymen got a dirty deal through the decision in England. This bill apparently has not been, submitted to the dairymen in the provinces, and certainly it has not been submitted

I have not received the answer yet that I am looking for. The provinces had nothing at all to do with the margarine decision. There was a great lobby put on to permit the sale of margarine in Canada; therefore the matter of the legality of legislation which permitted the sale of this so-called substitute for butter was submitted to the supreme court for a decision.

government of the province of Ontario as something that in their opinion would facilitate the enforcement of the law particularly with regard to the situation in the city of Windsor. There is one suggestion
I would like to make in connection with notice of appeal in general after conviction. It is a matter that sometimes arises where a conviction is followed by imprisonment in the penitentiary. The sentence does not commence to run until the accused actually is incarcerated in the penitentiary. The result is that numbers of accused who have been convicted sign waivers of their right of appeal; for, unless they do so, the first thirty days of their imprisonment will not count on their sentence. I suggest to the minister that injustice has followed the strictest application of that section dealing with waivers. Consideration should be given
[Mr. Coldwell.l
to allowing a convict to commence his sentence from the time he is sentenced rather than denying him that right and thereby constituting an inducement to him to sign a waiver of appeal. I know of a case, and I bring it to the attention of the minister, of a boy of eighteen or nineteen years of age who would have been acquitted on appeal, who signed his waiver in order that his time would count, and as a result there was more than a little difficulty in getting any action. I suggest that while it does not strictly come under this section, it is a matter to which consideration should be given.
I am very glad that provision is made for the right of an individual to secure an extension of time by the Supreme Court of Canada, following the expiration of the fifteen days. That is a salutary provision, and one that will assure the preservation of the just rights of an individual who, through inadvertence, fails to have his appeal launched to the supreme court within the period in question.

Mr. Chairman, from a hasty reading of this proposed amendment I would suggest that it is identical in substance with one moved yesterday in the committee by the hon. member for Kamloops. In other words, it purports to cover first the enemy at war; second the armed forces against which Canadian armed forces are contending where no state of war exists; and also, third, the country of the armed forces against which our armed forces are contending where no state of war exists. That was the point which was made by my hon. friends of the official opposition and which was passed upon by the committee in a motion, as I recall it, moved by the hon. member for Kamloops and which was voted down.
While this amendment may not be identical in language, I think it is identical in substance, and for that reason I still think we would be inclined to adhere to the clause as it was originally drafted. I shall not traverse the ground that I covered yesterday, because there would be no purpose in my doing so; but we have given most careful consideration to all angles of this matter, and we think that the inclusion in this clause of the countries of the opposing armed forces in Korea would be tantamount, as far as this bill is concerned, to acknowledgment of a state of war with those countries; for while we would be saying that it was not war, we would be putting those countries in the identical position in this clause in which we would put them were we at war with them.
We gave careful consideration to all these aspects of the matter when we were drafting this clause, and we must adhere to the language in which it now appears. I am afraid we shall have to oppose my hon. friend's amendment.

subtopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it strikes me that the clause as it stands is pretty wide; in fact I think it is wide enough to cover any situation that might arise. It seems to me that there have been cases in the past in which the forces of a country have assisted what we would consider to be a purely democratic undertaking within another country. This amendment might be interpreted subsequently in such a manner as to interfere with what were ordinarily considered to be civil rights and liberties.
Once this amendment is made to the Criminal Code it will be there for perhaps a long time. I think we should be careful not to put anything further along this line
Criminal Code
in the code, because we never know what may happen in this country in the future and who may be administering the code. I think the clause as it stands covers adequately the point that the government wishes to cover; indeed, even in this clause there are dangers should it be abused. Consequently I should be inclined to support the minister in letting it stand as it is. If I were going to amend it I would want more safeguards in order to make sure that the powers in the clause could not be abused, as I think they might be.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had hoped that when the time was reached to consider this the minister might accept this proposed amendment. In the first place, it meets the objection that was raised yesterday by one hon. member as to the wording; the words "military operations" are substituted. An important feature of the proposed amendment is that it makes it possible to deal with anybody who assists a country which is supplying troops who are fighting or who are engaged in military operations against our forces. The point made by the Minister of Justice is that we should not follow a course which amounts to an open declaration that we recognize an undeclared state of war created by the troops from that other country. I can only repeat what I have said before. We are not in any doubt that the forces now opposed to Canadian and other United Nations forces in Korea come from communist China. No one questions that. Not only do we know that from the identity of prisoners who have been taken; we know it from declarations by representatives of the communist government of China. I find it utterly inconsistent that in view of the tragedy that is taking place in Korea today we should be prepared to accept the illusion, created for their own satisfaction by the government of China, that these Chinese troops, veterans of the 8th route army, men trained by Russian communist instructors, are volunteers in the Korean forces. The thing is utterly unrealistic. The very best trained troops of the Chinese communist army have been thrown into action against the United Nations forces, which include young men from Canada.
I can only repeat what I have said before, that the time has come for us to say in no uncertain way that while we seek peace with China, we are not going to do anything to assist the Chinese nation under a communist government while that communist government is sending troops against our own young men. I hope this will be reconsidered.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) raised a point of order when this resolution was first presented to the house. If the house does not wish any further debate on the point of order, I am prepared to make a ruling now.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked whether it was in order not to set forth the maximum expenditure in a resolution preceding a bill "for any public aid or charge upon the people". I Iiave examined section 54 of the British North America Act and standing order 60. Neither of these provisions requires in terms that the maximum expenditure be set out in the resolution. Further, the citations in Beauchesne's third edition do not support the proposition. On the contrary, citation 439 indicates that the maximum expenditure need not be so specified.
I also have consulted the joint law clerks whose duty it is to prepare resolutions of this kind. They have informed me that there have been many instances in the past in which the maximum expenditure was not stated in the resolution, and also that in their view it is not always possible to assess the maximum expenditure. In these circumstances I have no alternative but to rule the present resolution to be in order. At the same time, however, may I draw to the attention of hon. members the following extract from Bourinot's parliamentary practice, fourth edition, at pages 404 and 405:
The cardinal principle, which underlies all parliamentary rales and constitutional provisions with respect to money grants and public taxes is this- when burthens are to be imposed on the people, every opportunity must be given for free and frequent discussion, so that parliament may not, by sudden and hasty votes, incur any expenses, or be induced to approve of measures, which may entail heavy and lasting burthens upon the country.
This extract suggests to me that it would be desirable, wherever possible, to include in resolutions' of this kind an indication of the expenditure to be incurred, although, as I have said, there is no positive legal requirement that this be done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion now before the house is in the usual form, asking the house to declare that it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Judges Act, 1946, and to increase the salaries of the judges other than the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. The resolution also seeks a declaration by the house that it is desirable to increase the number of judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario and the Superior

Judges Act
Court of Quebec, and to provide certain adjustments as to the pensions of judges and widows of judges.
I doubt very much whether any substantial measure of disagreement would arise as to the part of the resolution relating to the increase in the number of judges, because that is a matter of agreement between the provincial and dominion governments. I am sure also that in so far as those provisions seem reasonable to hon. members it is not likely there will be substantial disagreement in regard to such adjustments as may be made in connection with the pensions of judges and widows of judges. But from remarks already made in the house it would seem there is likely to be some discussion, and perhaps some substantial measure of disagreement on the question whether at this time it is expedient to introduce a measure that will increase the salaries of judges.
I think I should indicate that I presented to the government reasons why I hoped it would defer consideration of this bill until we meet again in October. Those reasons were not related to the merits of the provisions that are to be placed before us in connection with salaries. I pointed out that there will be a recess in the courts for a considerable part of the time between now and October, and that in any event it would be unlikely that the date on which any changes might become effective would be affected by letting this bill stand until the fall. I did suggest that there were reasons at this time why we should avoid any discussion that might give the impression that any member of this house was directly or indirectly reflecting upon the judiciary of Canada.
At a time when our whole society is threatened as it is today, I think it is appropriate to remember and seek to impress upon the house that our society is founded upon respect for our judicial system. That calls for a generally accepted belief in the minds of our people that the judges and judicial officers are impartial, competent, and beyond improper influence of any kind. Canadians have reason to be proud of the great tradition established in this country by the judges who have held those offices, in the Supreme Court of Canada, the supreme courts of the provinces or the various local judicial districts under their differing names in the different provinces. I think we have reason to be proud of the fact that since we became a nation in 1867 this country has been remarkably free of even the slightest hint of any reflection upon the men holding those high offices. It should be a source of satisfaction to all who believe in our free society that the judges, many of whom in

their earlier years were active partisans iir the political affairs of this country, have without exception, or almost without exception, recognized the great obligation they owe to society itself in accepting office. The records of our courts have been a tribute to the extent to which men and women can actively participate in debates under our democratic system and at the same time recognize that such debates in no way lessen our common acceptance of the obligation we all owe to Canada as a nation and to the society which has made our country what it is.
In every province and every local judicial district the judges occupy positions of very great importance, which go far beyond their ordinary judicial responsibilities. To a very large extent rthey are called upon to symbolize the impartiality and dignity of the law. They are called upon to occupy many voluntary positions of great responsibility in our general affairs, where the impartiality of their office gives them special qualifications which mean a great deal in the functioning of a free society. For that reason it is essential that the salaries paid the judges should be in keeping with the high office they occupy. It is important that the salaries should be such as to attract the best brains of the legal profession, those best qualified to perform these very important tasks. I feel sure the members of this house generally will approach this question from that point of view.
On the other hand there is a consideration which I do not think we should ignore at this time. Inflation, the changing value of the dollar and other circumstances connected with the unsettled days through which we are passing all have their impact upon the daily lives of all Canadians. I think the question must be faced squarely. If this high court of parliament is going to say to the people of Canada generally that we hope nothing will be done during this period of uncertainty which will increase the inflationary pressures, we should be prepared to defer any action which, by example as much as by the amount actually involved, might tend to have that very effect. I would hope that by October we may see the general economic picture more clearly than we do today. I would hope that we may see much more clearly what the real prospects are of international stability. I, for one, would not like at this time to say anything which might be interpreted as indicating any lack of recognition of the great importance of the position of the judges in this country, nor would I like to be put in the position of appearing to oppose appropriate recognition, in financial terms, of the great responsibilities

our judges do assume. On the of her hand, once again I place before the government the desirability of letting this matter stand over for three months so that we may not open the door at this time to any discussion which conceivably might unsettle the minds of the public in relation to the judiciary, or might involve decisions and arguments related to the present atmosphere of uncertainty which we would hope might to some extent be resolved by next October when we meet again.

That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Judges Act, 1946, to increase the salaries of judges, other than the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada; to increase the number of judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario and of the Superior Court of Quebec; and to provide certain adjustments as to pensions of judges and widows of judges.
I do not think this is the opportune time for the government to bring in a resolution of this kind. I do not believe that any of the judges today are financially embarrassed, but we have old age pensioners who can barely obtain the necessities of life. In my view we should look after those old age pensioners before we increase the salaries of the judges.
I am not saying they do not need it, or that they are not entitled to it. I do say however that at this time we should look after the old age pensioners first. When I saw this resolution on the order paper about six weeks ago I wondered whether the government was sponsoring it, or whether it was the minister. We know the farmer wants more for his wheat, and I was wondering if the bar association wanted more for the judges. Perhaps the minister will answer that question when he speaks.
The government, led by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), which has been preaching economy, which has been laying off staff from the post office and from other branches of the public service for purposes of economy, now brings in a measure to increase judges' salaries. I cannot understand it.
What do we hear repeated from the government benches? More production for wages received. I know, from my study of conditions in Canada for a long time, that some judges have far too little to do, while others are working much too hard. The latter group just cannot cope with the work they have to do. No government in Canada has at any time since confederation made a survey of the judicial districts; yet every ten years each government has looked over the redistribution so that each member of

Well, I can prove it to him, because I have been long enough around the courts of Manitoba to know something about what the judges do.

In my view this measure needs careful study. This would be a good opportunity to revise the judicial districts. I do not want to work the judges too hard, but I want them to give value for the money they receive. We look after them well; they receive good pensions. I am not objecting to their getting more money, if they need it. By all means give it to them, if it is necessary and if they deserve it. But this matter requires further consideration.

Let us look at the situation in the country. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) has mentioned the fact that we are preaching economy. That is what we are doing. Yet it is not only a matter of economy. It is a matter which involves the taxation of those who are less able to afford taxes in order to increase the pensions of those who need them less. Over and over again during this present session we have mentioned the necessity for some different financial policy in order to stop the rising cost of living. The rising cost of living hits everyone, especially the man who is on a low salary, the wage earner and the white-collar man.
The budget that we have just passed has increased the sales tax; and the sales tax affects the man in the low income brackets. Here we have two things: increases in the cost of living, and increased taxation for those who are already burdened. Then there is the increase in the income tax, or the surcharge. That is going to affect the taxpayer. Recently we passed the Old Age Assistance Act. That will once again increase the taxation of the people, because it is to be .partly a contributory scheme in the sense that an additional tax will be levied. That is the situation at the present time: increases in the cost of living, increases in taxation of this kind, that kind and the other kind. We have all that at the present time, and we are now proposing to increase the pensions of judges who now receive pensions of about $8,000 a year.
There is another reason why we believe we should not pursue this measure at this time. Much of the taxation that is now imposed upon the public is for defence purposes. If nothing would be done during this period of uncertanty to increase the inflationary pressure, we should be prepared to defer any action which by example as much as by the amount actually involved might tend to have that very effect." But there was a word of optimism at the end of his remarks when he said, "I would hope that by October we may see the general economic picture more clearly than we do today." No finer compliment has been paid the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) than the suggestion that after the budget has been in force for some months we may see the general economic picture more clearly than we do today.
I remember that in my family Sir John Macdonald was called "Old Tomorrow" because he was postponing all problems to the day after. My genial friend the leader of the opposition should not follow the footsteps of Sir John Macdonald. He is a man of action, and should decide today what is going to be done. What would be the difference if we waited until the fall? We will have a big session then, with all sorts of problems, and we have the opportunity to make a decision now.
CMr. Pouliot.]

Mr. Speaker, in common with other hon. members who have spoken, I recognize the importance to this nation of our judiciary. I recognize also the importance of our judges being free from economic worries so that they can do their best work in the administration of justice. I should like to make the point that there are many other people in the country who should likewise have more freedom from economic worries than is now the case. On that basis I contend that, in the matter of pensions, we should keep a sense of perspective.
The other day I argued, along with others, that we should remove the means test from the blind pension. It was pointed out that that would cost about $3 million, and that seemed to be one of the stumbling blocks. The member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) today pointed out to us that approximately $18-5 million is being spent on legislation and on the administration of justice, and he emphasized that that amounts to only one-half of one per cent of our national budget. I should like to point out that the $3 million that it would cost to remove the means test from the blind pension would be only eight one-hundredths of one per cent of our national budget.
With respect to pensions, we should bear in mind that the government is asking the older people of this country to accept an old age pension of only $40 per month. On the other hand, I ask hon. members to realize that our retired judges are receiving pensions on which it seems to me it is possible to live in a reasonable measure of comfort. As I look into the details that are provided in the book of estimates for the current year, I find that the pensions paid to judges, judges' wives and judges' widows, are listed in full on pages 207 to 210. I have not taken the time to make an exact count, but by looking over the list as carefully as I could in a few minutes, it seemed to me that about half or perhaps a little more than half of those listed in the estimates are receiving pensions of $5,000 a year or more. I want to make it clear that I arrive at that figure by grouping together a man and his wife wherever the two of them are living. There are quite a few cases where the retired judge is in receipt of a pension of $3,333 a year and his wife receives a pension of $1,667, which together make a pension of $5,000. I include all such couples in my statement that half or slightly more than half of those on judges' pensions are receiving $5,000 per year or more. There are a number who are

Judges Act
receiving $8,000 per year, and of course there is one at the top figure of $15,000 per year, and none of these judges made any contribution toward these pensions.
We do not know what the precise proposal of the minister is, in view of the fact that his resolution did not so indicate. The minister was supported technically by His Honour the Speaker this morning in the ruling he gave that he was not required by law to put that amount in the resolution. His Honour also said he thought it would be a good idea, whenever it was possible, to do that. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a case where it certainly was possible to put it in the resolution. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) smiling and shaking his head. I remind him that this whole business of whether or not to include in the resolution preceding a money bill the maximum amount to be involved, first started back in 1949 when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) brought in a resolution preceding a bill to amend the Old Age Pensions Act. He failed, on that occasion, to indicate the amount in the resolution, and he got into a bit of trouble in the committee because of it. The same Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he introduced the resolution preceding the amendment to the Old Age Assistance Act last week, put in the resolution the important figure of $40 per month. I feel that the Minister of Justice could have done that in this resolution. For my part I would say that what His Honour said about doing it where it is possible applies to this resolution.
At any rate, the newspapers have carried reports that the increase is to be in the order of twenty per cent. At a time when we are passing legislation to provide pensions of $40 per month for our senior citizens across the country, it seems to me the government is getting a bit out of focus when it asks us to agree to a twenty per cent increase in pensions of $5,000 per year or more. That means that what was a $5,000 pension will become $6,000. It means an $8,000 pension becomes $9,600 per year. We have not the bill before us, so we do not know whether these changes will be retroactive and will apply to judges, judges' wives and judges' widows now on pension or whether they will apply only to those who go on pension after the bill passes. Whichever is the case, the fact of the matter is that we are being asked to legislate for pensions which seem to me to go considerably beyond the demands of a comfortable retirement, particularly in comparison with what we are asking some of our other people to accept.

I recognize the need for increasing the number of judges in the Supreme Court of Ontario and the Superior Court of Quebec. But it seems to me that the pension provisions of this legislation are such that this house should turn them down. I agree with those who have pleaded with the minister to let this matter stand over until the fall. Perhaps the best way we could persuade the minister to do that would be to defeat the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair, and that would give the minister a chance to redraft the measure to meet the necessity for an increased number of judges without asking for pension increases for those who do not need them.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words that I want to say. I am opposed to that part of the resolution that proposes to increase the salaries and the pensions because I think that at this time they may well be considered to be substantial. I remember one of the ministers, on a former occasion, stating that it was necessary to maintain these salaries at a level that would permit our judges to live in a state of dignity. At that time I thought it was perhaps unfortunate that word was used, because I do not think that you can buy dignity. I do not think that dignity can be bought with money.
As a matter of fact, there are many people today who are living in a high degree of dignity on far less than the salaries that are paid to the judges. Then again, our judges do not need to worry about their old age. They receive a fairly substantial pension. There are, of course, some people who are receiving a fairly high salary who are not able to live in dignity because perhaps they over-indulge. If you increase the salaries of those people, the result certainly will not be that they will live in a greater degree of dignity. The result would be just the opposite. I recall a phrase that is popular in the English language, namely, "as drunk as a lord." What I mean is this. If you increase the salaries of people who are already indulging, it is not going to help the situation. I am not suggesting that is the case in this instance; but I point out that it is the wrong word to use. We should not use the word "dignity" in a case of this kind because dignity cannot be purchased with money.
The other point is that it would not be wise to increase the salaries of any group of individuals at a time when the government is trying to keep the cost of living down. As a result of the increase in defence preparations, we are all having to bear a part of that burden. If any one group of people in this

country are going to try to evade their fair share of the burden, it means that the burden of the rest of the people is increased to a corresponding degree. Of all the people in this country today, I think the one body of men who should not be guilty of that offence would be the judiciary. After all, you cannot expect the people of this country to respect any body of men who are not prepared to absorb their fair share of the burden of defence. Yet when any group of people at this time asks for or receives an increase in their salaries, they are trying to evade their responsibility, and to that extent they lose the respect of the people. We cannot afford to have our judiciary losing the respect of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker,
I approach this matter from the standpoint of a member coming from a distant part of our country. I find that a county court judge in Cariboo receives $6,666.66 per year. That is a substantial salary. But we must remember that he must pay in the neighbourhood of $1,100-I have not the exact figures-in income tax. As a result, his salary is reduced considerably. Let us say that it has been reduced until it is about $5,000. In 1871 the judge in Cariboo was getting $2,400, at a time when the cost of living was, of course, much lower than it is today and when we had none of the taxes which we have today. In that case I submit there is a good example of a man whose salary might be reviewed by this house.
The work of a judge in that part of the country would, of course, be quite different from the work of a judge in Ontario, in a settled part of the country. One of the judges I have in mind in my part of the country is continually travelling from one end of that large area to the other. He takes his car. He gets mileage on his car, of course; but he does not travel over the beautifully paved roads that exist in Ontario. He must travel over some extremely rough roads, and go into mountainous country and into difficult places. He gets the munificent sum of eleven cents a mile for the use of his car. I greatly doubt if that amount will see him through, having regard to the broken axles and other difficulties that he will encounter in the course of his labour.
He may go by plane to certain other places where he holds court. Hence you will see His Honour travelling by aeroplane; you will see him boarding the plane at two or three o'clock in the morning and travelling over the summit of the Rocky mountains which divide my county to the other point where court is to be held. He of course gets an allowance when he stays at hotels in these
Judges Act
various places. But after all, the life of that judge is not a pleasant one, in the sense of enjoying the ease, comfort and luxury suggested by the various speakers here. The same thing goes for the supreme court judges of British Columbia who must travel long distances, more often on the wing than not. They usually travel by plane from here to there.
Far be it from me, a layman, to come to the aid of the judiciary of our country in the presence of so many distinguished members of the bar. But I am a Canadian who would like to see the highest standard of excellence in connection with the bench; and I am Scotch enough and practical enough to want to pay a man at least enough to enable him to live in the same sort of dignified position in the community, let us say, as a member of the legislature or a member of the House of Commons.
Somebody said that judges were recruited from the list of defeated Liberal candidates.
I think that was the most unkind thing that has been said here all day. Again I speak only from my experience in British Columbia where we have some distinguished judges.
I think of the former judge in my own riding, namely, Hon. Fred Calder of Ashcroft, B.C., who did his duty there over a long period of years. He was a native of Nova Scotia, a man of great distinction and education, and he travelled by horseback, stage coach and so on, in the rain, in the sleet and in the snow, in good weather and bad, over all those years. He was a man who had never aspired to public office and who had taken no part in public affairs.
I think of ex-judge P. E. Wilson, K.C., of Prince George who in his day was an ornament to the county bench of British Columbia. I believe his court was established at Fernie or at Nelson; but he resigned his position in order to make enough money to educate his family. Now in his old age he is practising at Prince George. An extremely able counsel and a highly respected man is ex-judge Wilson. As a result of having resigned from the judiciary and getting himself a reasonably good income he was able to educate his family. Today a son of his, Mr. Justice Jack Wilson, is one of the outstanding supreme court judges of British Columbia and is, I am sure, a man whose ideals are much above the cash register and immediate emoluments. The younger Wilson has already distinguished himself in the public service not only in British Columbia but throughout Canada. He has presided at certain tribunals settling labour difficulties from coast to coast..

Judges Act
The present chief justice of British Columbia, the Hon. Wendell B. Farris, is a very distinguished native son of New Brunswick and a man of the highest character. He was not taken from the lists of the defeated candidates. An hon. member who says that goes out of his way to be offensive. Mr. Justice Macfarlane of British Columbia, Mr. Justice James Coady and His Honour H. J. Sullivan of New Westminster are men of the highest character. We have had outstanding men in British Columbia who had political experience. In what forum could they gain better experience than in the House of Commons? The name of the late Chief Justice Aulay Morrison, who represented New Westminster here in 1896, is "writ large" in the judicial history of British Columbia.
I am not going to speak at greater length, but I do suggest that if in 1871 a county court judge in Cariboo was worth $2,400 a year, when there was no income tax and when the cost of living was very low, and gold was worth less than $16 an ounce, before the general trend of rises in costs, expenses and so forth, it could certainly be established that a judge acting there in 1951 should be worth many many times $2,400 a year. Therefore as a layman I again say that I think it is the most outstanding thing in our system in Canada that a man without money or without position can come into our courts and find justice. If we are to maintain that sort of thing, then the honourable judges in Canada have to be placed at least on the same income status as the leaders in the commerce and business of our country, on a high level where they may fill a dignified position in their communities and be, as we would like them to be, among the leaders of culture and education in the life of Canada.

We have been debating this question for over two hours, I believe, and we are more or less debating it in the dark, as it were, because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has not done the house the courtesy of informing it what is involved in this resolution. Therefore, we must go on drawing our own deductions as to what may or may not be in it.
There are several parts in the resolution. Perhaps there would be no objection to some of them. The resolution provides for additional judges. I do not suppose there would be any objection in the house to making provision for additional judges, if the judges are needed-and as far as I am concerned I would take the word of the Minister of Justice for that.
There is a provision for an increase in the salaries of judges other than the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. There may be 
a case for increasing the salaries of judges other than judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, not because their salaries are not now high enough in relation to the salaries of other people in Canada, but because their salaries are being compared with the salaries of the judges of the supreme court who have had one or two increases during the last five or six years. For that reason I do not know whether I would be greatly concerned about a reasonable increase in salary, but then again there is the question of pensions. When I see a measure brought before this house asking for an increase in pensions for people who are already receiving pensions out of all proportion to those provided for the rest of the citizens of Canada I just cannot agree with it.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) referred to the salary of the county court judge in that area. If I heard him correctly, he said it was $6,666.66. That is the salary, but there is a pension for this judge, and for all other judges in that range of salary, of $4,444.44. After ten years on the bench-I believe that is the case-he can retire and draw this pension. Not only can he draw this pension but he can return to his law practice. Mind you, this pension is also non-contributory.

I appreciate the high position of judges in this country. I understand the high position they hold. I will accept the account of the hardships they go through in the discharge of their duties as recounted by the hon. member for Cariboo. But, sir, is that any different from what the ordinary John Doe in this country goes through? Reference is made to their travelling on planes, but what about the pilots, the stewardesses and the other people who are operating the plane? Surely their lives are just as important as the lives of the judges, and they are jeopardized every day when they take a plane into the air. I can take up the position of men and women in this country when I think of these things.
I have heard it said in this house that we should make financial provision for our judges in order that they may be free from temptation in the discharge of their duties. The moment we make that assertion we are by implication saying that the reason people get into trouble is that proper financial provision is not made for them. I do not think it is anything to anybody's credit when he avoids temptation just because good financial provision is made for him. What about the poor fellow who is brought before the judge? Ninety-nine times out of a hundred these people get into difficulties because of their

poor economic circumstances. In that regard I would like to read a short news item that came to my attention the other day which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of May 15, 1951. The headline of the article is: "Youths sing for police. Not dismayed by arrest." Then it gives the story of ten boys in their teens, ranging from 11 to 15 years of age, who were arrested by the police and arraigned in the social welfare court on charges of theft and receiving. The story goes on-told by one of the police officers who arrested the boys. He said this:
"We have to bring these boys before the courts, but I feel sorry for them," reported Detective Sergeant Thuot.
"They all come from poor families, each one with at least ten children. Most of their homes haven't got even the necessities of soap. These lads plainly suffer from poor environment."
I submit that before we begin increasing the salaries and pensions of those who can live sumptuously upon the salaries and pensions they are receiving, we should go about removing the conditions that bring young boys and young girls into court-conditions which start them on the road of crime from which there is no return. Those are the things to which we should be paying attention, but those are the things to which we are not paying attention.
When I compare the pensions paid to widows and wives of judges with the pensions that we placed upon our statute books only last week, where a man and wife are compelled to live on $480 a year provided they have no other income, not $5,000 a year, not $6,000 a year, not $15,000 a year, I realize that something must be done. The judges of our courts are conversant with these conditions because when they are not dealing with disputes between capitalist organizations this is the kind of thing which takes up their court time. They come in contact with men and women who never had a proper start in life because of the economic environment in which they were born and in which they are compelled to live.
I could say a good deal more, but I shall wait until the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) shows the house the courtesy of explaining the purposes of this resolution so that we may know what is involved. There is just one other thing though I would like to mention. I do not want to cast reflections upon judges because in so far as I have had the opportunity to meet them, and I am glad to say it has always been outside the courtroom, I have found them to be fine gentlemen. Observing them in the courtroom or the other places in which they have to discharge their duties, I think 80709-299
Judges Act
they have discharged those duties with credit to themselves and with benefit to the country. So I am not objecting to the resolution on that score.
I do object on the score that there should be this wide disparity in the incomes of people in a democratic country. It makes for conditions which, if not corrected in the ordinary process of parliamentary action- that is by bringing about a better distribution of income-will be corrected in other and less desirable ways. It has been mentioned that our judges are by and large political appointees. Surely no member of this house will say that that is not the case. I could take you to British Columbia and name for you one judge after another who was appointed because he had been defeated in an election. I do not say that a defeat in an election has anything in it that affects the character of a judge, but on the other hand I do not see anything in it that makes a person more fit to discharge the duties of a judge. I have mentioned a number of such cases in this house on other occasions.
I have another clipping from the Montreal Gazette. This is a newspaper which I do not think can be accused of being radical. It approves the increase in the salaries mentioned in this resolution on the ground of the increase in the cost of living. It mentions the chief justices in the provinces receive $13,300 which, as the former hon. member for Calgary West would say, is not hay. The judges of the superior court in the province of Quebec receive $12,000 each. Again that is not hay, but it looks pretty much like clover to most people. The editorial then goes on to say:
The proposed increases in the salaries of judges should have another important advantage. They will give the people of Canada a greater right to demand that judicial appointments be made among those notable for their judicial qualifications. Too often in the past appointments have been made mainly as a reward for political services-and they have often been made at a time when the value of these services has begun to wane.
The use of the bench as a place of political retirement should be ended.
Not only is it a political retirement; it is a place of political refuge and I agree that it should be ended. I suppose that as long as we have a system of competition where there is competition even among politicians and lawyers, there will be this never-ending struggle for existence and these cushy jobs will be given to those who have made a sacrifice by taking on impossible constituencies or by having served the party in some other acceptable way. I do not suppose we will get away from that, but we certainly should get away from putting certain men and

women on pedestals as it were and giving them positions of comfort and security to which not one one-hundredth of one per cent of our population can aspire. As I indicated, that is all I am going to say now, but when we know what we are really talking about I may have something further to say.

Mr. Speaker. I do not propose to go as far as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I would not say, however, that on the whole, I disagreed with the substance of his speech even if I did not fully approve of the words he used.
On the other hand, I feel that when a representative of a wage-earning group is called upon to vote an increase in salary to certain men in the professions, he should explain his stand. He is duty bound to do so.
I have never taken part in any class war. I have never objected to an adequate salary for any citizen according to his position, and I do not propose to do so today.
In 1932, I approved the increase in the salary of recorders in the city of Montreal. I remember that the salary of the chief recorder was then raised from $7,000 to $9,000 a year. That was during the depression. But my duty was clear-cut and I did not hesitate for one moment, even in the provincial legislature. When the committee on private bills examined the bill relating to the city of Montreal, I endorsed the measure, although I represented the labouring class, the low wage earners.

Mr. Speaker, as stated by several of the previous speakers, one must take into account the standard of living that a judge must maintain, no matter in what court he sits. I agree with the hon. member who said that our judges should be paid enough to achieve complete security when they reach middle age or even old age. I know that a large number of very eminent and competent lawyers would never accept a judgeship since they earn far more through their private law practice. Therefore, in order to have good judges-and I am speaking now with full knowledge of my responsibilities, on behalf of my constituents who are intelligent enough to understand-we must give them a salary which is sufficiently high to attract to the bench good lawyers who thus will be assured of security.
Still I feel it to be my duty to speak of other people who are in receipt of government pensions and of the way in which they are treated. I have nothing to say against the present government. They have done more than any other government in the field of social security. Still, I have been told that there is no limit to good deeds and that though we may keep on doing them for as long as we wish, there always remains something to be done.
Well, Mr. Mayor ... I beg your pardon; I am so used to speaking at the city hall that I used the expression Mr. Mayor. Mr. Speaker, if ever there was a class of people -I have always spoken in their defence- who should have received special consideration from our leaders, it is that of the white-collar workers.
Some people, who are always in favour of salary increases in the other spheres of the administration, never consider the salaries of certain department heads or certain leaders-I am not referring to any member of the house-and when we state the views and requests of this class of small salary earners, they become so very careful. It is only with the greatest caution that, when forced to do so, they grant a slight salary increase.
While I congratulate the government for what they have done up to now, I hope they will deal further with this class of white-collar workers.
As other hon. members have said, we recently allowed a certain increase in the old age pensions. It is all to the good. But here again we must consider-and I believe it is my duty to call the attention of govern-80709-2991

ment to this matter-whether it would not be fitting to improve further the condition of our older people.
We are not unaware that, although judges' widows are also assured of a pension-which some may find inadequate, while I personally find it inopportune-they are nevertheless secure from want and care.
On the other hand, without leaning towards exaggerated socialism I wonder if the widow of the worker is assured of sufficient income when her husband dies rather young, as often happens.
These measures deserve to be considered by the government. As I said, I want it to be well understood that I am wholly and entirely in favour of these measures. Mr. Speaker, I had at first thought that I might discuss this matter to better advantage for all concerned after the text of the bill was before the members so that reference might be made to the various clauses of the bill as they related to my remarks. But I must say that I was rather impressed by the objections raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) that on this resolution it is but fair that some general outline of the contents of the bill should be given in advance in order to inform hon. members whether they should vote for or against the resolution. For that

Judges Act
reason I should like to make a few remarks of that general nature and, if I can, dispel some of the wrong ideas that are entertained concerning the measure by opposition speakers.
Reference has been made to the increase in judges' pensions which are supposed to be authorized in this bill. The bill provides or will provide-if indeed it is proper for me to refer to it at all in this debate-for an increase of 20 per cent across the board for judges in the county courts and in the supreme courts of the various provinces, and in the Exchequer Court of Canada; but not in the Supreme Court of Canada because of the fact that last year an increase was granted to the judges of that court.
As I am sure hon. members are aware, the judge's pension is not established as any fixed amount. It is two-thirds of his salary.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARIES AND NUMBERS OF JUDGES
speechtext:
The increase in the salary will affect the pension of all those who go on retirement after the time that this bill goes through. But there will be no increase in judges' pensions as such; that is to say, there will be no increase in judges' pensions which are now being paid to those who were retired before this bill comes into effect. In that sense, therefore, there is no increase at all in judges' pensions, except in the future; and then not in the pensions as such but in the pensions arising out of the increase in the salary.
In addition to this salary increase there are three other provisions. I am referring now to these pension arrangements and salary arrangements. The first is one which I think no member of this house will oppose in spite of the views he may have voiced in the debate this afternoon. It is to authorize the grant of an annuity to widows of judges who died before August 15, 1944, being the date of the coming into force of the (provision enabling judges to elect to divide their annuities between themselves and their wives. For some time after judges' pensions were granted, they were made payable only to the judge himself and expired with the judge's life, leaving his widow with no interest in the annuity which had been payable as a pension to her deceased husband for his life. It was represented that in many cases-and these are some of the distressing cases with which we are now confronted- that arrangement left the widow of the judge in penury because, in spite of the fact that the salaries which the judges receive may 
seem large to those who earn less, it is a fact that quite a large percentage of the widows in whose favour no division of the judge's pension had been made before August 15, 1944-because no such division could be made-are now in extremely necessitous circumstances.
When the question arose as to what provision could be made to deal with the problem which had become apparent from the concrete examples of these destitute judges' widows, it was suggested to the judges that each judge would be permitted to elect, when he received his pension, whether or not he would retain the whole of it payable to himself, for his life, to expire on his death, or whether on the other hand he would agree to have his judge's pension divided up into three parts, turning over one part to his wife and retaining the other two-thirds to himself. If a judge who had made such an election predeceased his wife, she would continue to draw her one-third share of his pension for her lifetime, and in that way would be provided for. But if the wife predeceased the judge, he would draw not his whole pension but only the two-thirds of it which he had reserved for himself by his election.
As I say, this arrangement went into effect on August 15, 1944. Before that date no such privilege of election was available to the judges, and there are now over one hundred judges' widows in different parts of Canada, some of whom we know, from representations that have been -made to us, are in distressed financial circumstances. With regard to that group it is proposed that we shall be enabled to pay to the widow an annuity not exceeding two-ninths of the salary provided by the act for a county court judge-in other words, two-ninths of the-smallest judicial salary-that was paid at the date of the deceased judge's death. That comes to quite a modest sum, but it can be paid only provided that she can establish that she is in necessitous circumstances and has not remarried.
The second authorization is that to pay annuities to widows, in substantially the same circumstances, of judges who retired on pension before August 15, 1944, and who have since died. That is, they retired before the time at which they could make that election and have since died, leaving widows in necessitous circumstances. In other words, these widows fall in the same category as the first group and are included in the estimate of 100 or more to which I referred a moment ago.
Then, the third provision is to authorize a judge who retired on pension before August

15, 1944, and who is living today, to elect to divide his pension between himself and his wife. There is just the one pension. When he divides it, it means that his widow, in the event of his death, will continue to get one-third. But if she predeceases him he will draw only his two-thirds. Therefore the cost to the treasury of providing for this election is not great. It is a matter of disposing of the pension in a way that will take care of both of them during their joint lifetime and of the survivor during the survivor's lifetime.
So far as salaries or pensions are concerned, all that the bill contains is a 20 per cent increase in salary across the board, but no increase in judges' pensions as such, and then this other provision of pension for widows, and the provision authorizing the judge who retired before August 15, 1944, to make the election where he had not previously made it.
There will be no dissent in this house from the sentiments which were voiced by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) when he opened the debate on this resolution today to the general effect that a strong and independent judiciary is the very keystone of our constitutional system. When we talk about our various freedoms, our civil liberties, our freedom of the press, our freedom of speech, our political freedom and all of these other attributes which we democrats are privileged to enjoy as very few people in mankind's history have been, we must realize, if we reflect upon the matter, that under our constitutional system these freedoms are guaranteed to us by the independence of the judiciary. Without it they would be unenforceable.
The first thing that any dictator does when he wishes to destroy these liberties is to gain control over and make the judiciary subservient to the executive. Democracy as we know it, the rule of law as we know it, can be traced back to the time when our British ancestors were able to establish the principle that the king was "under God and the Law"-the law as interpreted by judges independent of the executive. Therefore when we make a judicial appointment we take upon ourselves a very great responsibility, a responsibility that I may say, speaking for myself, and I am sure that is true of all my predecessors in the office which I hold, I have at all times felt very keenly.
We are rather inclined to take the bench for granted, because we have an able bench. We have never needed to worry about their independence; we have never needed to worry about the manner in which they
Judges Act
carried out the duties of their office, as to how they have protected our liberties. We take the judges for granted in the same way that we take liberty for granted; but I can assure you that if the conditions in that respect had been different from what they have been, we should then be, I think, perhaps a little more appreciative of the all-important function which the judges perform in our society.
The other night I took home the file of a poor chap who was sentenced to death for a capital crime to consider there his application for commutation to life imprisonment. When I took this file and read through the evidence in order to form judgment as to whether a commutation should be granted, which for that poor man meant the difference between life and death, when I read the role which the judge played in those proceedings and stopped to think that this was a man whose appointment I had recommended about a year ago, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a matter of great satisfaction to anyone in these circumstances if he can see, as I was able to see on that occasion, that the judge had a full grasp of the whole course of the trial, that he was able to render a proper disposition of the points of law which arose, that he had grasped the salient facts, leaving one who read that transcript with the feeling that here was a case where the life of a man was at stake and where it was in just, honourable and competent hands.
It is our duty in the Department of Justice -one of the most important duties that we have there-to try to get men who have the ability, the integrity and all the other necessary qualities to judge a case of that sort where a man's life may be at stake, or where a man's reputation may be at stake, or his honour, or the interests of a community, to say nothing of large sums of money from time to time. In seeking, as we have sought, able men-and I wish to repudiate the unworthy suggestion which was made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), I think it was, to the effect that we appoint no one to the bench but defeated candidates-I would have been prepared to say perhaps the day before yesterday that we would have great difficulty in finding defeated candidates to put on the bench-I do not think that the record of this or any other Liberal government if examined will support the hon. member's imputation. Not only are those who have been defeated in political contests a very small percentage of the appointments to the bench, but-and I will not name them- some very eminent Conservative lawyers have been appointed to the bench, which they now adorn, as the hon. member for

Judges Act
Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) was fair enough to admit when he spoke this afternoon.
No person who approaches this responsibility which I have in the Department of Justice with any proper consideration of his duties can afford to ignore this realistic fact, that one problem is that in a time like the present it is not hard at all to get very competent counsel to accept a position upon the bench at much less indeed than what they are then earning. But the figure has to be somewhere within striking distance of their income as lawyers. This is not because these men are mercenary or grasping, for many of them make substantial financial sacrifices in order to take on the honourable duties of a judge which they would not make if they had that attitude.
As we all know, these men after a long period of good income earned by very hard work have been accustomed with their families to a certain level of expenditures. I do not mean that that is because they are purse proud at all, but, as we all do, they develop a certain way of life. There is not one of us in this House of Commons who does not acquire in the course of his life certain commitments arising out of his home, children in school, friends and the like. Each of us can modify our plans and expenditures within certain limits, but if the Department of Justice is going to get the best men for the bench, as I think we should, we have to have those limits within reach of the best counsel. As one who has a fair measure of responsibility in this matter, I say to hon. members of this house, and I think those who are fair will be inclined to agree, that there would be nothing worse for the administration of justice than a strong bar and a weak bench.
What are the facts in this connection? Since 1920 up to date, over 30 years, the judges of this country have had one increase in salary. If the increases proposed by this bill go into effect they will have received in relation to what they were earning in the year 1920 an increase of 60 per cent. That is not 60 per cent compounded; that is 60 per cent on the 1920 figure. If we assume that the salaries which they were then receiving were not excessive, if we assume that they were fair-and I think I am safe in saying that they certainly were not higher and were indeed lower than most comparable salaries paid in other countries of the British commonwealth and the United States that derive their parliamentary and legal systems from the same sources we do; they were much lower than the salaries there-we must remember that the solitary increase which the judges have already got 
plus what we are proposing here, represents an increase of only 60 per cent on top of those salaries.
Let me read to the house figures which indicate the increases that have occurred in the incomes of other economic groups in this country during the same period of time. I have before me a table prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics dealing with the wage rates in this country and covering a period from 1921 up to the present. The year 1939 is taken as the base year with the figure 100. On that basis the 1921 index is 97-5 and the preliminary index for 1951 is 225-5. In other words there is an increase in that period, not of 60 per cent as there will be for the judges if this bill goes into force, but of 125 per cent.
I also have before me a table showing the details of farm cash income from 1926 to 1950, the base being 100 in the year 1926. This table shows that in 1950 the farm cash income had risen to 235-5.
