This is cash income, after taking care of costs.* This table does not include any supplementary payments which may have been made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We do not need to stop with that group. The same thing can be demonstrated in connection with the income of other classes or groups in the country. These are facts which are well known to all of us. These figures merely indicate what has been taking place all around us in these various economic groups during that period.
For example, the salaries of public servants have risen from time to time through the efforts of their associations. Because of their associations one would naturally expect these increases to be more rapid than those of the judges who have no organization. The judges because of their position cannot conduct collective bargaining as they have no organization for that purpose. They remained from 1920 until 1946 without any adjustment in their salaries at all. That is not in keeping with what should be our concept of their position. It is true they have had security, they have had pensions and they have had a dignified position, but they have had no increase in that time.
I am not referring to their dignified position in the sense in which the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) did; I refer to the dignity that arises from the high and honourable office which they hold. But it is a position which they cannot demean by a display of miserliness when for example the collector

for the community chest comes around or in relation to other claims of that sort. There is the matter of maintaining a status which I think the hon. member for Acadia will agree is not a matter of being dignified by mere money in the sense in which he was using that term.
Then I come to the average weekly earnings in nine leading non-agricultural industries including forestry, mining, manufacturing, construction, transportation, public utility operation, trade, finance and services. The year 1939 is the base year and the preliminary figure for April 1951 is 206 -6. It may be more interesting to note that this table shows that the index of earnings in this important category in 1946 stood at 138 -6. There has been an increase from 1946 to the present time, five years, to 206-6.
I could go on indefinitely making comparisons of this sort and indicate that the judges, because of the positions that they occupy and their inability to raise the question of salary upon their own behalf, have not been in a favourable position to get adjustments from time to time. They have had only one increase since 1920 and if they get the present one will be receiving a 60 per cent increase as compared with increases of nearly twice that amount received by all these other economic groups. I know that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) can cite these distressing cases which appear before judges, and there is not a member of the house who will not agree with him in the sympathy that he feels towards those who are unfortunate. But when the bargaining representatives of a union-and I have dealt with quite a number of them on occasions when I was at the head of the public utilities of Manitoba-come to discuss what is fair compensation for the work they are doing for society, it is not that they feel callous towards the oppressed but they do not raise the question of the oppressed in discussing what would be a fair wage for the work they are doing for the employer for whom they are working. With great respect, I do not think they should do that, because what we should do in relation to the oppressed is to help them and lift them up; but we cannot administer our society, we cannot run our industry, without negotiating with the employees to pay them a fair wage for the work they are doing.
So far as a group is concerned who have no bargaining powers in that sense, it should be our responsibility to see that they do not have to come to us, that we will be fair because they cannot come to us, and we should see that they are taken care of in the same way as these other groups. This has

been realized by a number of different groups who are interested in these matters. I think reference was made to the fact that the bar association would naturally want to support an increase in judges' salaries. That is a very natural assumption, and it is the case. But we have not had the representations confined to that group by any means. A statement of the problem with which we are concerned here, and which I think is perhaps the most cogent we received from any source, was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on October 4, 1949, going on to two years ago, by Mr. Percy Bengough, C.B.E., president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. This is what he said:
The executive council of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, at a meeting in Calgary following the convention, considered the question of judges' salaries. We fully realize that this is a matter somewhat outside the jurisdiction of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. However, we are of the opinion that those directly concerned are in a more or less difficult position to advance their claims.
That is precisely the position. They are in a difficult position, and because they are in a difficult position they went from 1920 to 1946 without any adjustment at all. Show me any other group in Canada of whom that can be said.

I think that is all I should like to say at the moment except that before I sit down I should perhaps make a reference or two to the points raised by previous speakers in the debate. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), a fellow Manitoban, says that some judges are too busy and others are too idle. As is so often the case, I agree with the hon. member. He is quite right when he says that. But, Mr. Speaker, under the division of authority under the British North America Act the appointment of judges to the provincial courts is the prerogative of the federal government. After they are appointed everything they do is under the direction of the attorney general of the province, who has exclusive authority over the administration of justice and everything pertaining to it. I do not say this in any way to shuffle off responsibility upon the provincial attorneys general. On occasion I have been acting attorney general myself for fairly long periods of time, and I know what is the difficulty in this connection. It is a fairly simple matter. There is a certain distribution of population in the year 1900, we will say; there are certain centres of importance, and judges are stationed there. There is a redistribution of the population of the province, and in relation to other centres the population in the original centres becomes less. But the judges still stay there, and the provincial administration will simply get hades from the people of those areas if they seek to move resident judges from their midst. Many of the representations made to me privately by those whose acquaintance with judges seems to have been confined to the county court judge in their own community, with whom I suspect they have been doing too much fishing, have been along this line: Why should we increase the salaries of those . judges when this judge I know never has very much to do, as far as I can see? Mr. Speaker, by a vote of 11 to 5 in the committee on miscellaneous private bills the subject matter

of this bill has been returned to the House of Commons. This is the second time this bill has been up for second reading, the subject matter thereof having been sent back to that committee on the previous occasion. So we have before us this bill, the evidence relating to which I hold in my hand, asking for the granting of a divorce for the relief of one whom I will call Mr. X. 1 do not know Mr. X personally nor do I know Mrs. X, but I am sorry for both. I should like to help them both or either of them, if it lay within my power to disentangle the skein into which their lives have become tangled. Great as may be my interest in the troubles of these particular people mentioned in Bill No. 232, there is something that even transcends that interest, and that is my desire that the honour and dignity of this House of Commons be preserved.
I believe, sir, that in the stress and strain of our lives here, in the tedium of routine and in the bickering of daily debate, we are inclined, through our closeness to what we are doing, to lose sight somewhat of the importance and greatness of our task which I conceive to be the moulding and welding of this young country into a great nation. We have here a great tradition. The mantles of great men have fallen upon our shoulders. I suggest that tradition has its drawbacks and dangers as well as its advantages. Precedent has begun to harden into tradition in this house. A precedent which was established, and has continued by expediency, has over the years begun to harden into tradition in the matter of the consideration or lack of consideration of these divorce cases like the one in this Bill No. 232 in which Mr. X is suing for divorce. These cases emanate from provinces which have no divorce courts of their own. Those are the provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec, notedly the province of Quebec. Thus it is that tonight we are considering this Bill No. 232 in which Mr. X is suing Mrs. X for divorce. One of the greatest heritages of this country, which explains to some degree our virility, is the mixture of races that we have.
We have great statesmen in our tradition. We have great parliamentary traditions behind us. We have the Pyms and the Hampdens, the Gladstones and the Pitts. The French have their great statesmen, some of them translated to this soil, like Cartier and Laurier. Those of United States origin have their Washingtons and Lincolns. I am, in all seriousness and earnestness, asking hon. members to ask themselves what those statesmen, who have handed on all these glorious parliamentary traditions, would think of us tonight if they knew we were stooping to the consideration of Bill No. 232, a case for

the divorce of Mr. X from his wife; that we were turning this great parliamentary-institution into a mere divorce court, because a mere divorce court it is. There is no question about that.
Sometimes I think, perhaps it is a presumptuous thought, that there may be in this parliament at this very moment men whom posterity may some day call great. I am sure that you, sir, with your characteristic modesty would deny that title as applied to yourself, but there are those who may think otherwise. Some of the men whom I have mentioned were not considered great by their contemporaries, either, and it was only time that elevated them in the esteem of succeeding generations. Some of them were great parliamentarians. They mapped the course of great nations. They laid down the paths that we should follow. I would suggest that the path we are following tonight is not one of the paths they intended us to follow.
Here we are considering Bill No. 232. I would ask if this great forum of the Canadian people is to be turned into a divorce court. I wonder if there is any other parliament anywhere that has stooped to such a procedure. We are the representatives of the Canadian people, sent here for a totally different purpose. In considering divorce cases we are attempting to handle work for which we are not at all fitted. Some of us may be fitted for it. There are clever lawyers in this house, but I am not one of them. Are we to descend to listening to these tales of knocking at bedroom doors, to devoting our time to hearing about investigators prowling up darkened stairs and sticking scotch tape on the outside of doors? Are we to descend to the unfolding of divorce drama on the stage of Montreal boarding houses, listening with unwilling ears to this sordid and conflicting evidence, produced in many cases by professional investigators who take that way of earning their living.
It is becoming the custom in this house, and certainly in the private bills committee, not to consider these bills at all in the ordinary sense of the word "consider". The practice has grown up, as you, sir, very well know, of passing these bills en masse, forty or fifty at a time, without even the formality of reading the numbers. When my hon. friend the chairman of the committee started consideration of these bills tonight, he had to be told to read the numbers, and naturally so because that is not the custom which he has been following. We in this house are sick and tired of that procedure. It is my belief that all the members of this house are sick and tired of that procedure, probably including the sponsor of these bills, our genial chairman of the private bills committee. The
Private Bills-Divorce
perpetuation of this backdoor method of granting divorces is to me a sign of political and national immaturity.
In dealing with this bill I am not here entering into a discussion of divorce at all from a moral point of view. There are those whose religious beliefs teach them that divorce is wrong. I respect those views. I respect the men that hold those views. The province of Quebec does not desire to have divorce courts set up within her boundaries. That is completely within the rights of that province, and those rights must be respected. But the individual rights of the citizens of this province to come here and obtain a divorce in the only manner that is presently available to them must also be respected. I suggest to you that there are two courses open to us: first, to continue this method of turning this house and the private bills committee into a divorce court. If we are going to do that, then some of us feel that we must accept the responsibility a little more than we have done in the past. We shall have to give to those bills the proper consideration so that we can pass upon them without violating our consciences. We shall have to weigh the evidence in each case before passing judgment.
There are objections to that course. In the first place this is not a judicial, but a legislative, body. Careful study of each of these cases would take up most of the time which we now devote to the passing of legislation.

I probably did not interrupt hon. members at the beginning of the session, but now that the session is drawing to a close, and there are other private bills on the order paper, I think hon. members should confine their remarks to the particular bill which is before the house.

There are certain faults that I have to find about the consideration of even this bill which had a certain amount of consideration before the committee on miscellaneous private bills, extending over two or three hours. For I submit that even that amount of consideration, where some of the gentlemen did not even have the evidence in front of them, was something of a farce. I think we should get rid of this particular bill. As a matter of fact, I am going to suggest that we get rid of it; and having said that, I hope I may be permitted to suggest that we should get rid of all these particular bills, including Bill No. 232. Such a method, of course-and it is a method that has been proposed by my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-would be to allow these bills to go before some other court such as the exchequer court sitting in Ottawa.
Order. I do not think the hon. member should stray too far away from the principle of this bill. I would ask him to direct his remarks to the principle of this bill.

I think I should perhaps be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to defend my remarks
IMr. Knight.)
about the Senate with regard to this bill; because when I am commenting upon their actions in regard to this bill, I want to make it perfectly clear that I am making no reflection whatever upon those gentlemen. I believe that this bill had a thorough and complete investigation by the Senate committee; and I believe that they gave their judgment in accordance with their views. It may be a tedious and thankless task. That committee is made up of sensible men. Some of them are lawyers. I am sure that they were able to handle this bill by a proper method. It was suggested that it might be left entirely in their hands. So far as I am concerned, I should like it if this Bill No. 232 had never come out of the Senate; I should be glad1 that, if necessary, their decision should be taken, and that we should not have been bothered with it. But having been bothered with it, and having felt the responsibility of looking into the evidence in connection with this Bill No. 232, I have come to the conclusion that this Bill No. 232 is a case in which there is a reasonable doubt at least as to whether Mr. X should receive a divorce from Mrs. X, his wife.
I promised that I would come directly to the bill itself and I have a word to two to say upon that. The group to which I belong has insisted that we give this bill thorough examination.

May I ask the hon. member a question?
' Mr. Knight: Not just at the moment. I have had some of the hon. gentleman's questions in the miscellaneous private bills committee. It is my privilege, as I understand it, to answer or not to answer questions put by the hon. gentleman, at my own pleasure.
As I say we have given, and we intend to continue to give, full consideration to these bills. Our limited examination of this bill and others has slowed down but little the passage of these bills through the house. I admit that I am slowing down the passage of this one to some extent tonight. I refer to this particular Bill No. 232. But heretofore we have not held up any bill because we felt that to do so without notice would not be fair. These are bona fide people who have paid their fees in these particular cases, and who have come through the House of Commons miscellaneous private bills committee. Then for them not to get the divorce is something we do not think would be fair, without due notice.
In this case we have seen to it that there was a discussion. As a member of the House of Commons it is my privilege to ask that a

Private Bills-Divorce
certain procedure be followed, Since we are a divorce court, this bill must be examined by the house. It is my privilege to ask for a vote upon this bill, and I intend to exercise that privilege. Those of my hon. friends who are opposed to the passage of this bill, being opposed to divorce in general as a matter of conviction, and whose custom it has been to oppose these bills merely by shouting "on division", will now have the opportunity to be counted and registered by name as being in opposition. When this bill comes to a vote, those who are not perhaps necessarily opposed to the principle of divorce will have an opportunity to express their disapproval of the procedure by which this bill has been handled. One might say that that is a rather drastic procedure as far as the principals of this bill are concerned. But I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is one bill as to which there is a reasonable doubt; and if there is a reasonable doubt, that doubt should be for the benefit of the respondent and not for the petitioner.
In voting on this bill there is yet another class of hon. members to be considered. I know that some of my hon. friends on the other side of the house, my colleagues in the particular divorce committee-that is a short name I have for the miscellaneous private bills committee-have considered this bill carefully. I know that they are convinced that this bill for divorce should be granted. So those gentlemen, this third class of people, will have an opportunity to vote on this bill, and to vote in favour of it.
In regard to the passage of bills like this one through the house it has been said-and I think the suggestion came from my friend the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir)-that these bills should be considered in detail in the miscellaneous private bills committee and not in this house. I therefore want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, how this particular bill, No. 232, was handled in that particular miscellaneous private bills committee. You will remember that the subject matter of this particular bill, not the bill itself, was referred back to that committee. I shall break no confidence here and I shall tell no secrets because the proceedings of that committee are open to the public. This bill, No. 232, the petition of Mr. X for a divorce from his wife, was considered on June 13 at ten o'clock. On the orders of the day there were three classes of item, three private members' bills, religious bills and the like, and there were 123 divorce bills which had received second reading in the house, and then there was the subject matter of this particular bill which was to be considered. The three private bills were called, and I want the house
to note that in each case there was a sponsor or parliamentary agent to explain the bills to the committee. Then came the 123 divorce bills, all of them. I did protest to my colleagues-and they will bear me out in this- I did protest and objected to the way these bills were being handled in that committee. I do want to say here, and I want to put it on the public records, that we did not hear a reviewing of the evidence in any of those bills. With this protested bill it was different. Members of the committee asked some questions of lawyers who appeared, one for the petitioner and one for the respondent. At the end of that time, having in some cases considered the evidence before, certain of the members were beginning to see what were the facts in regard to this particular bill.
I might say that the 123 bills which were not up for second reading, but had been referred to the miscellaneous private bills committee for examination were passed by that committee without being read by name or number or by any other method. These 123 bills passed in exactly two minutes by my wrist watch, a procedure which affected twice 123 or 246 principals, and probably a greater number of children. Just two minutes were taken in the miscellaneous private bills committee for that purpose, and I shall challenge any of my hon. friends on the other side of the house who do not approve tonight of what I am doing here to dispute that statement.
Now, to come to the bill itself and the reasons why I say that this is a bill upon which we can safely centre our protest as to the method used. It is a bill, the opposing of which will create no great hardship on anyone. I shall put on the record the reasons why I take that stand. I know that there are some of my hon. friends in the committee who do not agree with me in that regard, but that of course is their privilege. From this study and from the review of the evidence by the lawyers in question I would like to submit the following reasons why this bill should not be passed. I am talking about Bill No. 232 now before this house for second reading. I have written down, sir, and with your permission I shall read the six reasons that I have here as arguments.
One, that some of the evidence is contradictory, and what evidence is not contradictory, is quite inconclusive; two, that the husband had applied for annulment some years before but that it had not been granted to him; three, that when both of these people, the petitioner and respondent in this case, had applied for a legal separation in the civil courts it was to the respondent of Bill

Private Bills-Divorce
232 and not to the petitioner that such separation was granted; four, that the manner of the woman's life had been brought about to a degree if not totally by the desertion of the husband in the previous years; five, that he was alleged to have left his wife alone and deserted and without care when she was seriously ill; six, that the motive for bringing the application for divorce would appear to be-I say in my opinion-a desire to evade any further payment of the weekly allowance which the husband had been compelled to pay to his wife under the legal separation to which I have made reference.
Now, sir, those are the reasons why I think this is one bill which we can oppose without creating any great hardship on anyone. In making this case, sir, of course I say I have no legal training. I presume that is readily apparent. I can simply state the things in this bill as I see them. One of the less kind of my hon. friends suggested in the committee that I was quite ignorant of legal proceedings. Exactly; that is just the point I want to make, and I have already confessed to it. I said that he was unkind, but he was kinder than he knew, because he made the exact point that I wish to make, namely, that we are not qualified to act as judges on Bill No. 232, or any other divorce bill, at least I am not; and yet it is one of the things that I have to do. It is one of the things with which I have to reconcile my conscience; it is one of the things for which I have to take the responsibility, this breaking up of a home. How then can we act as judges in a case like this about which we know nothing except in so far as the lawyers were able to rehash the evidence? But we did not see the witnesses. We could not judge of the kind of people they were. We had no idea how reliable their evidence would be except from the stories, contradictory, that we heard in the evidence. How then can we pass judgment upon cases of which we know nothing?
Sir, I do not think that a case like this Bill No. 232 should be a case of A suing B for divorce in order that it may be out of the way so that the case of C versus D could come up. It seems to me that, in a case of this sort where there are human beings involved, and where there are often children, divorce judges, like the judges in a juvenile court, should have special qualifications for the work which they are doing, understanding, interest and sympathy, and some knowledge of psychology, and above all an interest in bringing these people together again, this Mr. X and his wife mentioned in Bill No. 232, in making an attempt to patch this broken marriage before the granting of a 
divorce, and only when it is seen and admitted that that divorce is inevitable should divorce be granted; and finally there should be some regard to any children of such a union.
Would any hon. member in this house venture to say that this particular institution of the miscellaneous private bills committee approaches the ideal which I have been painting as to what a divorce court should be? For as things stand, this is a divorce court dealing with Bill No. 232, the case of Mr. X and Mrs. X, his wife.
Carried.

I shall be finished in just one minute. I am now going to move a motion. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, and before I move this motion may I say that we procrastinate on this thing from year to year. That is why I am moving a motion on this particular bill. I think we shall have to come to an end by refusing to approve of the method that we are using in this Bill No. 232. We must no longer be unwilling to face this issue, no longer unwilling to grasp this nettle, because the vacillation that we are indicating here is not the stamp of a great parliament, of a united nation, but is, as I have said, the sign of immaturity national and political. Let us rid ourselves of this undignified pretence; let us rid ourselves of this scourge and get on with the work that we were sent here to do.
I oppose this bill, Mr. Speaker, and I move, seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy):
That the word "now" be deleted, and that the words "this day six months hence," be added at the end of the question.
In opposing this bill, Mr. Speaker, may I say this in conclusion: I can do no other. Were I to support this bill, and were it to pass this House of Commons, I should have it upon my conscience that through such action here we will have accomplished one thing only-
I do not think you have any.

If we pass this bill we shall have accomplished one thing, namely, we shall have deprived this woman of her only means of sustenance, a woman who is past middle age, broken in health and who has already suffered much. Let other hon. members of this house, let my hon. friends who have interrupted me tonight who are secure in their livelihood, and doubtless in their own integrity, think well before they cast at her this final crushing stone.

Mr. Speaker, I aim to be brief. We are not here to discuss

the whole matter of divorce proceedings. This bill is simply following a precedent which has been set in parliament while the hon. member who has just spoken at length was here for many years. This petitioner has come to parliament in accordance with the usual practice. He has had to pay to have this bill presented, he has had to pay his lawyers and so forth.
I am not going to review the evidence in this case because the galleries are occupied, but a Senate committee which had as chairman a gentleman skilled in the law, which had as a member a gentleman skilled in medical science, has found that there was sufficient evidence of adultery to satisfy it. Then a committee of this house re-examined that evidence and a majority of that committee-we had a standing vote-felt that there was definite evidence of adultery. No reasonable man could come to any other conclusion but that these two at three o'clock in the morning, considering the way they were dressed or undressed, had been guilty of adultery.
There was ample evidence to support the petition and a committee of this house adopted the bill. Therefore I am against the motion. If my hon. friend wants to change the divorce laws of the Dominion of Canada, this is not the way to go about it. The proceedings in this case were the same as the proceedings in other cases which other hon. members of his group have countenanced for many years. In view of the fact that the Senate committee and a committee of this house have examined the evidence in connection with this bill, and in view of the fact that there is ample evidence to satisfy any reasonable man there was adultery, I submit that the petitioner is entitled to his divorce.

Mr. Speaker, it would appear to me that the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) has his wires crossed in respect to the evidence he has been reading. Perhaps he has been reading evidence in another case. I do not think the evidence of the case before us would indicate the things that he states. I rise to support the motion of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight).
Over the years I have spoken in this house on a number of occasions on these divorce bills. I want to point out from the start that I am not against divorce provided the statutory grounds have been proved. But I do insist that before any divorce bill passes this house I must be satisfied that such grounds for divorce have been proved.
The hon. member for Yorkton has eulogized somewhat the qualifications of certain members of the other house who sit on the Senate
Private Bills-Divorce
divorce committee and attempt to exercise their good judgment. I agree with the hon. member that they are men of integrity; I agree that some of them are men of legal ability; but that does not mean that this house must swallow their decisions holus-bolus. Even the best jurists misjudge at times.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver)
suggested on one occasion that some of us were not skilled in legal matters. I must confess that I am not skilled in legal matters, but when it comes to reading evidence and attempting to discover from the evidence whether grounds for divorce have been proved I submit that it does not take a legal mind to discover whether proof has been made. As a matter of fact I think sometimes the legal mind can overlook some human elements that enter into cases such as those that come before us.
Oh, oh.
Order.

It is all right; the hon. member was not tapping his desk, he was knocking his head. I stand with the hon. member for Saskatoon in his motion to give this bill the six months hoist. I do so on the ground that the reason for divorce has not been proved in this particular case. I have gone through the evidence rather carefully and I am perfectly convinced in my own mind that the hon. member for Saskatoon is right when he draws the conclusion that the petitioner is simply seeking to absolve himself from responsibility in connection with the terms of the judicial separation which involves the payment to the wife of a certain amount for her support.
I notice the clock states that it is nine o'clock and I move the adjournment of this debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

That the time for the consideration of private bills be extended this day until eleven o'clock p.m., or such earlier hour as the remainder of the same still appearing on the order paper have been disposed of.

Private bills come up for consideration in the house on Monday afternoon and from 8 o'clock to 9 o'clock on Tuesday and Friday evenings. By general consent the hour may be extended, but if objection be taken, the house must go on with the other business on the order paper.

I fully realize, Mr. Speaker, that the citation might lend itself to two interpretations.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I believe it is after nine o'clock.
Order. The hon. member has risen on a point of order and I think I should hear him.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT Canadian maritime commission-
531.	Steamship subventions, as detailed in the estimates, $3,779,875.

Before the dinner recess I was about to ask the minister for a statement under the general heading of Canadian maritime commission. The minister promised a statement on the policy for the present year with respect to the Canadian deep sea shipping industry as well as a statement with respect to the North Atlantic planning board for ocean shipping. The matter was brought before the minister on May 17 by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. No report has yet been supplied to the house, and I should like the minister to make a statement.

I wonder if we could have that in the next item. It has to do with the transfer and subsidy policy. This item is for steamship services. If we could pass it, perhaps I could make a statement on the next item.

Item agreed to.
532.	Assistance tor Canadian flag ocean shipping industry, $375,000.

With reference to the North Atlantic planning policy, at the request of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I did make a statement which I placed on Hansard, and I think perhaps it will not be necessary for me to deal with that again now. With reference to the maritime commission, I tabled the annual report some days ago- perhaps it was yesterday-but for the hon. member's information let me say that general conditions with reference to world shipping are far better now than they have been for quite some time. As a matter of fact the world shipping situation has undergone a complete change, and this has been of great benefit to the deep sea shipping industry. The change can be attributed to a variety of reasons including increased international tension, the increased need of ships for transporting facilities and supplies to the Korean theatre of war, the sudden need in

the latter part of 1950 for additional bottoms for the movement of coal and other commodities to Europe. That has brought into great demand ships of the Liberty and Park types of which Canada has a substantial number. Canadian owners operating these ships have had substantial profits in the last period.
With reference to the subsidy policy, there is only one application which has been made for transfer of flag from Canada to the United Kingdom. If the hon. member will look at the supplementary estimates he will see there a small item to cover the remaining ships. I think an amount of $3 million was set aside, following the announcement of policy made by the Prime Minister, to care for some forty ships at the rate of $75,000 each. Some thirty-seven applications have been made and approved of, although the amount of the subsidy has not been paid in each of these cases. There remain some payments which are being looked after by the supplementary estimates.
With reference to the replacement plan, it has worked out very well. There is a substantial amount of money in the escrow fund, and this money has been used on numerous occasions for the construction of ships. Not only in the great lakes shipping area but also on the Atlantic coast and the Pacific coast there are owners who have taken advantage of the replacement plan and have constructed a number of ships varying from large ferry vessels to large lake carriers. In fact one of the largest lake carriers ever to be built in Canada was launched at one of the upper lake ports on Saturday of last week. The transfer policy has worked out very well, and I think because of it, it can be said that the position of the operators is better today than it was at the time it was instituted. At that time there were some 37 or 40 ships out of employment. Today there are none, in fact there is a scarcity of bottoms at this time. Generally speaking I think that is the position in so far as the transfer and subsidy policy is concerned, and the replacement plan, the subsidy policy and the position of the escrow fund.

Then do I

May we have from the minister an authoritative statement as to the relation^ ship between this northwest communications system and the northwest communications system which is operated either by or on behalf of the Department of National Defence. In the .public accounts committee some two or three weeks ago we spent an hour or more one morning going over the public accounts in relation to the northwest communications system as reported in the public accounts of that year under the Department of National

Defence. Therefore I am wondering if the minister has the information on which to make an authoritative statement on the nature of this system in his department and the relationship between it and the system under the Department of National Defence.

This system was constructed by the United States government and taken over by the Canadian government by virtue of what was known as the Ilsley-Morgen-thau agreement of 1944, together with the Canol project and other projects in the Northwest Territories and the northwestern part of Canada. These assets were turned over to Canada for operation. This northwest communications system is operated by the Canadian National Railways for the use and on behalf of the Department of Transport, and this amount of $100,000 is a capital expenditure for additional facilities required on the system. In other words it is working capital for the land line system facilities in operation in that area.
Is this in connection with the Alaska highway? Is this a telephone and telegraph system on the highway itself?
It is.
And it does not serve the military installations at all?
Only to a limited extent.
It is chiefly a highway communications system?

That is right.

I have had a telegram and letter from the maintenance of way union in my railway centre asking for some sort of assistance, a bonus or something of the kind, in view of the high cost of living. If this were given it might avert another strike or something of the sort. All over the system, particularly on the Belleville division, a great many maintenance of way men have been laid off. On one branch line they have been cut down to almost half. This is really disrupting the men and the service. The men were laid off. I think each man has five miles of track to maintain, whereas previously he had three and a half miles. Can the minister tell us anything about that?

May I point out to the hon. gentleman, Mr. Chairman, that this is a vote for the administration of the Department of Transport, and therefore has nothing to do with the operation of the Canadian National lines. The Canadian National Railways budget was placed before the committee on railways and shipping some months ago, and passed. In so far as the Canadian National Railway is concerned, I am not able to discuss it on this item.

I shall be glad to bring it to the attention of the Canadian National Railway officials.

I do not imagine that it would be felt to be expedient that the committee be reconvened at this session, but I would ask the minister whether he is in a position to give any consideration to the 80709-300
Supply-Transport
matter, and whether it is intended to bring it before the house at the next session?

The matter to which my hon. friend refers has just recently been brought to my attention. I took cognizance of the recommendation made by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, but I have not yet had an opportunity of discussing it with the chairman of the board of transport commissioners. I think I should, through courtesy to him, ask for his views. In any event, I am not in a position to say whether or not an amendment to the Railway Act would be required. If it is, consideration would have to be given to whether an amendment should be included along with the other amendments that are being made to the Railway Act. Personally, I do not think it should because the amendments that will be introduced at the fall session are those having to do with the report of the royal commission on transportation.
